By the time Apollo 11 had went to the Moon in July 1969, public support for the program had already begun to fade. Polls from the mid-1960s show that a majority of Americans thought the money would be better spent elsewhere, and the 1968 budget was the first to cut NASA's funding.

The landing is remembered as a moment of unity, and for one evening it was. But the astronauts returned to a country that had largely made up its mind, and the last three planned missions were cancelled within two years. Engineers who had spent a decade on the Saturn V found there jobs gone by 1973.

The program did not end because it failed. It ended because it succeeded and nobody had decided what success was for.
